steps: Sign of x²: positive opens upward (minimum), negative opens downward (maximum).
Roots: where the curve crosses the x-axis (y = 0). Factorise or read them off.

method_card.title: How to Work with Quadratic Graphs
method_card.content:
A quadratic graph is a U-shaped (or arch-shaped) curve called a parabola, given by \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\).

If \(a > 0\) it opens upward (minimum); if \(a < 0\) it opens downward (maximum).

The roots are where the curve crosses the x-axis (\(y = 0\)); the turning point is the vertex.

steps: The turning point x is still \(x = \frac{-b}{2a}\), but now use the real value of a (for example 2a = 4 when a = 2).
For the max or min value, substitute that x back into the full equation. That y is the answer, not the x.
Root facts: the roots sum to \(\frac{-b}{a}\) and multiply to \(\frac{c}{a}\); the turning point x is the average of the roots.
gold.title: Gold: when the x² coefficient is not 1

example.question: Find the turning point of y = 2x² − 12x + 10.

steps: A quadratic \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\) draws a parabola: a U-shape if a is positive, an arch if a is negative.
To find y at a value of x, substitute: square the x, then work out the other terms and add. Watch the sign when x is negative.
The y-intercept is the constant c (set x = 0). A root is where y = 0.
bronze.title: Bronze: read one feature off the curve

example.question: For y = x² − 4, find y when x = 3 and give the positive root.

steps: Roots: factorise \(x^2 + bx + c\) into two brackets, then set each to 0. Two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.
Turning point: the x-coordinate is \(x = \frac{-b}{2a}\) (or the midpoint of the roots). Substitute it back for the y-coordinate.
If a is positive the turning point is a minimum; if a is negative it is a maximum. Its y-value is the min or max value.
